platforms.title: Why Isn't the AirPods Hearing Aid Feature a Real Hearing Aid?
platforms.meta_description: The FDA cleared AirPods Pro 2's Hearing Aid Feature in 2024, the first OTC hearing aid software. What the trial found, and where the feature falls short.
platforms.body_html:
In September 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration authorized Apple's Hearing Aid Feature for AirPods Pro 2 through the De Novo pathway, the first time the agency had cleared an over-the-counter hearing aid software device. Headlines made it sound like AirPods had simply become hearing aids overnight. The clearance is real, but the fine print matters more than the headline, and it changes how much you should rely on the feature.

What the FDA actually reviewed

The clearance covers a software application running on iPhone and iPad, not the earbuds themselves as a standalone medical device. That distinction matters because it defines exactly what was tested and for whom. According to the FDA's own summary, the authorization rests on a clinical study of 118 participants with self-perceived mild to moderate hearing loss. The study compared people who self-fit the device using the app against people who had the same device professionally fit by an audiologist, and found comparable perceived benefit between the two groups. Audiologists generally don't dispute the feature's usefulness; the point they make is that it was studied as a self-fitting aid, not as a replacement for a full clinical hearing evaluation.

What Happens When You Fix This — the Checklist That Actually Matters

First, know that the clearance is bounded to mild-to-moderate hearing loss. The clinical evidence doesn't extend to severe or profound hearing loss, where a professionally fitted hearing aid is calibrated far more precisely for an individual's audiogram than a self-fitting app can manage.

Second, remember the built-in hearing test only measures how loud a sound needs to be before you hear it — it does not diagnose why hearing dropped in the first place. Noise-induced loss, middle-ear infection, and other causes all look similar on a simple threshold test, so a passing grade on the app tells you almost nothing about the underlying cause.

Third, speed matters if hearing loss appears suddenly in one ear. The American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery's clinical practice guideline recommends offering corticosteroid treatment within two weeks of symptom onset for sudden sensorineural hearing loss, since the chance of meaningful recovery drops the longer treatment is delayed. A reassuring app result is not a reason to postpone an ENT visit if hearing loss came on suddenly.

Fourth, mind how long you wear them. Earbuds aren't built for all-day wear the way a fitted hearing aid is — prolonged sealing of the ear canal raises the risk of outer-ear infection, so take them out before bed and give your ears a break if they start to feel damp or itchy.

None of this makes the feature useless — for many people, it lowered the barrier to even noticing a hearing problem, something they'd otherwise put off checking for years. But treat a good result as a reason to keep paying attention, not as a medical clearance, and treat a bad or uncertain one as a prompt to book an actual hearing test rather than a second opinion from the same app.
